title: Accounts Receivable and Aging Reports

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe accounts receivable and its role in the medical practice revenue cycle.
- Interpret aging reports to categorize outstanding balances by age.
- Identify overdue accounts and prioritize follow-up based on aging.
- Apply professional follow-up and collections concepts while protecting confidentiality and escalating within scope.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of AR like a pile of IOUs from people who owe the doctor money for care they already received.

### Question 2

If your neighbor borrows your bike and promises to return it, that promise still has value to you — AR is the practice's “you owe me” list.

### Question 3

Charging for a visit is like writing a new IOU that gets added to the pile, making the “you owe me” list bigger.

### Question 4

Paying off part of a loan shrinks what you still owe — posting a payment shrinks the patient's outstanding balance the same way.

### Question 5

If you give a cashier too much money, the register owes you change — a credit balance is the account owing “change” back.

### Question 6

AR is like a bank account that only changes in three ways: new bills (charges), money in (payments), and price corrections (adjustments).

### Question 7

It is like timing how long a lemonade-stand customer takes to pay you back after they buy a cup — shorter is better.

### Question 8

If everyone who buys your lemonade takes months to pay, you still have to buy lemons and sugar today — that squeeze is a cash-flow problem.

### Question 9

A clean claim is like a homework paper with every answer filled in and no eraser smudges — the teacher can grade it right away.

### Question 10

You check a garden for weeds often so they don't take over — the practice checks AR often so unpaid bills don't pile up.

### Question 11

If AR is the list of people who owe YOU money, accounts payable is the list of people YOU owe — two opposite stacks.

### Question 12

After insurance pays its share, the part left on the table for the patient to pay is the “you owe me” slip the practice tracks in AR.

### Question 13

AR starts the moment the work is done and the bill is sent — like starting a timer when you hand over the goods.

### Question 14

If you are owed $120 and people normally pay you $4 a day, it takes about 30 days to collect it all — that is what “30 days in AR” means.

### Question 15

Cash flow is about having money in your pocket now; a big stack of unpaid IOUs doesn't buy supplies until someone actually pays.

### Question 16

It is like sorting a pile of unpaid IOUs into folders labeled “new,” “a month old,” “two months old,” and so on.

### Question 17

The report lines up bills the way you'd line up overdue library books: due now, a month late, two months late, and so on.

### Question 18

The “current” column is the fresh mail in the mailbox — it has not had time to become late yet.

### Question 19

If a bill is six and a half weeks old, it goes in the “1 to 2 months” folder, not the “this month” folder.

### Question 20

The longer a friend takes to return your game, the less likely you'll ever see it again — old debts are the same.

### Question 21

You rescue the tray of cookies closest to the edge of the table first — the oldest debt is closest to being lost.

### Question 22

If you borrow a book and a game from a friend at different times, each item is overdue by a different number of days.

### Question 23

It is like a kitchen sink that keeps draining — fresh water (new charges) flows in but does not back up into a clog.

### Question 24

If a leak suddenly gets worse, you tell the plumber and find where the water is coming from — you don't just mop forever.

### Question 25

You check the weather each morning, not once a year, so you can grab an umbrella before you get soaked.

### Question 26

It is the coach's scoreboard — the billing team and manager watch it to decide the next play, not the fans in the stands.

### Question 27

You track money a friend owes separately from money the school cafeteria owes — each needs a different reminder.

### Question 28

If the bill is about three to four months old, it lands in the “three to four months” folder on the aging report.

### Question 29

The friend who pays you back in a week is faster than the one who takes three months — lower days in AR means faster payback.

### Question 30

It is a checklist of the bills that have been waiting the longest, so you know which ones to call about first.

### Question 31

A brand-new bill isn't scary, but a bill sitting unpaid for four months is — age is what makes a debt risky.

### Question 32

It is like sorting laundry into whites, colors, and delicates so you know which load to wash first.

### Question 33

If only one of your friends never pays you back, the problem is probably with that friend, not with your notebook.

### Question 34

The taller the “very overdue” stack of IOUs, the more the practice guesses it might never see that money again.

### Question 35

You'd rescue the ice cream melting longest from the freezer first, even if it isn't the biggest tub.

### Question 36

It is like a line at the grocery store that keeps getting longer — the cashier isn't checking people out fast enough.

### Question 37

You'd figure out why your library fine is wrong before you just give up and pay it — investigate first, write off last.

### Question 38

If your chores take 30 minutes instead of an hour, that's progress — lower days in AR is the same kind of good news.

### Question 39

A bill becomes “late” once its due date passes — overdue means the due date has come and gone.

### Question 40

To find the overdue books, you look at the shelves past the “due this week” section.

### Question 41

You catch the glass nearest the edge of the counter first, no matter whose glass it is.

### Question 42

You'd return the phone call that's been waiting the longest first — the 150-day balance has been waiting the longest.

### Question 43

A denial is like a form returned for missing a signature — you fix the form and send it again, not send a “pay up” letter.

### Question 44

It is like a letter you mailed two months ago with no reply — time to check whether it was received.

### Question 45

If you've sent two notes and heard nothing, it's time to actually talk to the person.

### Question 46

The friend who's had your bike for four months with no plan to return it is the one you flag, not the one who borrowed it yesterday.

### Question 47

It is like a homework assignment with a hard deadline — if you're about to miss it, you tell the teacher (manager) right away.

### Question 48

If the cashier gave you too much change, the fix is to give it back — not to ask for more.

### Question 49

If the same plant keeps wilting, you don't keep watering it the same way — you try something different.

### Question 50

If the delivery said “5 days” and it's been 10, your package is late — a claim is overdue the same way.

### Question 51

A statement is the note that says “here is your bill — please pay this amount.”

### Question 52

It is like a friendly monthly reminder to return what you borrowed — a single reminder is easy to forget.

### Question 53

It is like agreeing to pay for a bike in five weekly chunks instead of all at once.

### Question 54

The manager holds the “yes” stamp for payment deals — the assistant can collect information but not stamp it alone.

### Question 55

A write-off is when the practice finally says “we won't get this back” and crosses it off the list.

### Question 56

You only throw away a lost item after you've really searched everywhere for it — write-offs happen after the searching is done.

### Question 57

Asking nicely and explaining the bill is like a neighbor politely reminding you about a borrowed ladder — not yelling about it.

### Question 58

Your money matters are private — you wouldn't want the whole neighborhood told how much you owe.

### Question 59

After insurance pays its share, only the leftover slice is yours to collect — not the whole pie.

### Question 60

If you're handed too much change, the honest move is to give it back — the practice does the same with overpayments.

### Question 61

You wouldn't drive an hour to return a nickel — sometimes the trip costs more than the money.

### Question 62

It is like turning up the reminder volume slowly — a note, then a call, then a knock on the door — not starting with the knock.

### Question 63

It is like keeping a notebook of every time you asked to borrow something back — so everyone knows you really tried.

### Question 64

You wouldn't tell a stranger how much money is in your neighbor's wallet — billing details are private the same way.

### Question 65

When a question is too big for you, you hand it to the grown-up in charge — that is what referring up means.

### Question 66

Follow-up is like checking on a package that hasn't arrived — you find out what happened and fix it.

### Question 67

It is like writing down “called the bank Tuesday, spoke to Sam, resending the form Friday” so you don't lose your place.

### Question 68

If your homework comes back “wrong,” you fix the mistake and turn it in again — you don't hand in the same wrong paper.

### Question 69

A tickler is like a sticky note on the calendar that says “check on this account on Friday.”

### Question 70

If someone says a receipt is wrong, you check with the person who can see the whole picture, not just erase it yourself.

### Question 71

To track a package you check the shipping website — to track a claim you check the payer's portal.

### Question 72

You leave a note that says “please call me back” instead of taping your private business to the door.

### Question 73

If the store undercharges you for change, you check the receipt and ask — underpayments get checked the same way.

### Question 74

The assistant can gather the papers, but the manager is the one who argues the case.

### Question 75

You'd pay the bills that are almost overdue before the ones due in three weeks — age tells you what's urgent.

### Question 76

If the librarian says your form is missing a signature, you add the signature — you don't pretend the form is complete.

### Question 77

Writing down “said she'd pay Friday” lets you check on Saturday whether she did.

### Question 78

When someone is upset, you stay calm and say “let's look at it together” instead of shouting back.

### Question 79

One is chasing the insurance company for its share; the other is chasing the patient for their share — two different doors.

### Question 80

If the repair shop says “it'll be ready Friday,” you still check back Friday — you don't assume it's done.

### Question 81

The assistant runs the reminder calls and keeps the notes; the big decisions belong to the people in charge.

### Question 82

Missing the deadline on a contest entry means no prize — missing a filing deadline can mean no payment.

### Question 83

When you have one watering can and many plants, you water the one that is wilting most.

### Question 84

If your friend says they never got your note, you double-check the address before you get annoyed.

### Question 85

You check the price tag against what you paid to see if the cashier short-changed you.
